title: India Beat Germany 3-1 to Seal Best Women's Hockey World Cup Finish in 52 Years
excerpt: Navneet Kaur's brace powered India to fifth place at the FIH World Cup in Amstelveen, their best showing since the inaugural 1974 edition.
body:
• India defeated World No. 5 Germany 3-1 in the 5th-6th classification match at the FIH Women's Hockey World Cup in Amstelveen, Netherlands.
  • Navneet Kaur scored twice (44th and 47th minutes) while Ishika opened the scoring in the 43rd minute as India dominated the third quarter.
  • The fifth-place finish is India's best at the Women's Hockey World Cup in 52 years, bettering their results since finishing fourth in the inaugural 1974 edition.
  • The squad, featuring 11 World Cup debutants under captain Salima Tete, lost only once in the entire tournament — to hosts and Olympic champions Netherlands.

India's women's hockey team signed off from the FIH Hockey World Cup Belgium and Netherlands 2026 with a statement victory, dismantling World No. 5 Germany 3-1 in the fifth-sixth place classification match in Amstelveen on Thursday. The result secured India their best finish at the Women's Hockey World Cup in 52 years — since they placed fourth in the inaugural edition at Mandelieu, France, in 1974.

For a squad featuring 11 World Cup debutants, the achievement carries weight far beyond the final scoreline. Coach Sjoerd Marijne's team suffered just one defeat across the entire tournament — a 0-2 loss to hosts and Olympic champions Netherlands in the second round.

Third-Quarter Blitz Breaks the Deadlock

The first half was a cagey, tactical affair. Germany enjoyed more possession in the early exchanges but struggled to convert territory into clear chances. India grew into the contest, with Baljeet Kaur and Sakshi Rana combining effectively down the right flank. Captain Salima Tete nearly latched onto a cross in the opening minutes, but the German defence held firm.

"For a squad featuring 11 World Cup debutants, the achievement carries weight far beyond the final scoreline."

Germany earned multiple penalty corners in the first half but failed to capitalize — sloppy injections and miscommunication repeatedly let India off the hook. At the other end, Navneet Kaur tested German goalkeeper Finja Starck three times in the second quarter, but each effort was turned away.

The match turned decisively in the third quarter. In the 43rd minute, Ishika broke the deadlock with a composed reverse-lift that beat Starck cleanly. Just 60 seconds later, Navneet Kaur doubled the advantage, converting a penalty corner with a sharp touch-and-slap finish. India were relentless — in the 47th minute, Navneet struck again, dribbling past the goalkeeper and lifting the ball over her for a commanding 3-0 lead.

Germany's Late Consolation Falls Short

With three goals to chase, Germany pushed hard in the final quarter. India dropped into a disciplined defensive shape, absorbing pressure and clearing their lines with purpose. Goalkeeper Bichu Devi made two important saves in the closing stages to keep the Germans at bay.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=aG-FtcqltuQ

Lynn Krings finally pulled one back for Germany in the 59th minute, converting a rebound, but it was too little, too late. India held firm to seal a 3-1 victory and fifth place.

A Tournament to Remember

India's journey through the 16-team tournament was marked by resilience. In Pool D, they opened with a 2-2 draw against China on August 16, hammered South Africa 6-1 two days later, and ground out a 0-0 draw with England on August 20.

The second round in Pool E proved tougher. A 0-2 defeat to the Netherlands on August 21 was India's sole loss, and a goalless draw with Australia on August 23 narrowly ended their semi-final hopes. But the team regrouped for the classification match and produced their best performance of the tournament when it mattered most.

What This Means for Indian Women's Hockey

India's World Cup history has been patchy at best. After their fourth-place finish in 1974, they failed to qualify for several editions and rarely threatened the top tier of the competition. A ninth-place finish in 2022 was their most recent result.

This fifth-place showing — achieved against a German side ranked four places above them — signals genuine progress. The team's performance at the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, where they reached the semi-finals, appeared to mark a turning point, and the World Cup result confirms the trajectory is holding.

India will look to carry this momentum into the Asian Games, which begin next month. Their opening match is against Indonesia on September 19, with the team expected to be among the medal favorites.

For the Indian diaspora worldwide, the result is a rare moment of pride in women's hockey — a sport that has long lived in the shadow of cricket. With a young squad gaining major tournament experience and delivering under pressure, the future of Indian women's hockey looks brighter than it has in decades.
